organic: Apply neem oil spray (5ml/L of water) every 7 days until symptoms reduce.
Use copper-based organic fungicide (Bordeaux mixture 1%) as preventive foliar spray.
Apply Trichoderma harzianum bio-formulation (5g/L) to soil and foliage.
Spray diluted baking soda solution (1 tbsp/gallon) to raise leaf surface pH.
chemical: Spray Mancozeb 75% WP at 2.5g/L of water every 7-10 days.
Apply Chlorothalonil 75% WP at 2g/L as preventive contact fungicide.
Use Azoxystrobin 23% SC at 1ml/L for systemic control in severe cases.
Alternate fungicide groups to prevent resistance buildup.
mechanical: Remove and destroy infected lower leaves immediately upon detection.
Prune dense canopy foliage to improve air circulation between plants.
Apply organic straw mulch (5cm layer) around plant base to prevent soil splash.
Use drip irrigation instead of overhead watering to keep foliage dry.
biological: Apply Trichoderma viride bio-agent (5g/L) as soil drench and foliar spray.
Use Pseudomonas fluorescens (10g/L) as seed treatment and foliar application.
Introduce Bacillus subtilis bio-fungicide for competitive pathogen exclusion.
Apply compost tea (fermented 48 hours) as foliar bio-stimulant.

spray.best_time: Early morning (6:00 – 9:00 AM) before temperature rises
spray.evening_alternative: Late evening (5:00 – 7:00 PM) after heat subsides
spray.wind_warning: Do not spray if wind speed exceeds 15 km/h to prevent drift

prevention: Practice 3-year crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops (legumes, cereals).
Use certified disease-free seeds and healthy transplants from nurseries.
Maintain proper plant spacing (60cm between plants) for adequate air circulation.
Apply organic mulch around plant base to prevent fungal spore splash from soil.
Remove and destroy all crop debris and volunteer plants after harvest season.
Avoid overhead irrigation — use drip or furrow irrigation systems.
Apply preventive fungicide spray at first flowering stage before symptoms appear.
tips: Inspect lower leaves weekly — Early Blight always starts from the bottom of the plant.
Water at the base of the plant early in the morning to allow foliage to dry before evening.
Prune lower suckers and branches touching the soil to reduce infection pathways.
Keep a crop diary noting when symptoms first appear to plan preventive sprays next season.
Rotate fungicide chemical groups (M3, 11, 7) every 2 sprays to prevent resistance.
early_blight.source: ICAR-Indian Institute of Vegetable Research; APS Plant Disease Compendium; Cornell University Plant Pathology

organic: Apply copper hydroxide fungicide (2g/L) immediately upon first symptoms.
Spray Bordeaux mixture (1%) every 5-7 days during wet weather conditions.
Use potassium bicarbonate (3g/L) as foliar spray to suppress sporulation.
Apply compost-based bio-fungicide with Bacillus amyloliquefaciens.
chemical: Apply Metalaxyl + Mancozeb (Ridomil Gold MZ) at 2.5g/L for systemic + contact action.
Spray Cymoxanil + Mancozeb at 3g/L every 5-7 days in epidemic conditions.
Use Dimethomorph 50% WP at 1g/L for curative systemic treatment.
Emergency: Apply Mandipropamid (Revus) at 0.6ml/L for immediate stop-spread.
mechanical: Immediately remove and destroy all infected plant parts — do NOT compost.
Improve field drainage to eliminate standing water near crop roots.
Install raised beds or ridges to improve soil drainage and reduce humidity.
Use plastic mulch to reduce soil moisture evaporation and splash.
biological: Apply Trichoderma harzianum (10g/L) as preventive soil and foliar treatment.
Use Bacillus subtilis strain QST 713 (Serenade) as bio-fungicide.
Introduce beneficial mycorrhizal fungi in soil to enhance root disease resistance.
Apply fermented plant extracts (garlic + chili) as natural anti-fungal deterrent.

spray.best_time: Early morning (6:00 – 8:00 AM) — critical during wet/humid weather
spray.wind_warning: Avoid spraying during wind; Late Blight spores spread rapidly by wind

prevention: Plant certified Late Blight-resistant varieties (e.g., Kufri Jyoti for potato).
Avoid planting tomatoes and potatoes adjacent to each other in the same field.
Destroy all volunteer potato tubers and tomato seedlings before planting season.
Monitor weather forecasts — apply preventive fungicide before humid/rainy spells.
Ensure good field drainage and avoid low-lying waterlogged planting areas.
Use pathogen-free seed potatoes from certified sources only.
Remove and burn all infected plant material immediately — never compost.
tips: Late Blight can destroy an entire field in 7-10 days — act immediately at first sign.
Dark water-soaked lesions with white fuzzy growth on underside of leaves confirm Late Blight.
After heavy rain or fog, scout your field within 48 hours for new symptoms.
If more than 30% of foliage is infected, consider emergency harvest of unaffected produce.
Report confirmed Late Blight outbreaks to local agricultural extension services.
late_blight.source: International Potato Center (CIP); USDA ARS; Cornell Late Blight Decision Support System

organic: Spray copper oxychloride 50% WP at 3g/L every 7-10 days.
Apply neem oil (5ml/L) combined with copper for synergistic bacterial control.
Use acidified copper spray (add citric acid to maintain pH 5.5 in spray solution).
Apply Bacillus-based bio-bactericide as preventive foliar spray.
chemical: Spray Streptomycin sulfate (500ppm) + Copper oxychloride (3g/L) combination.
Apply Kasugamycin 3% SL at 2ml/L for systemic antibacterial action.
Use Copper hydroxide 77% WP at 2g/L as contact bactericide.
Alternate antibiotic sprays with copper to prevent bacterial resistance.
mechanical: Remove and destroy infected leaves and fruits — do not touch healthy plants after.
Disinfect pruning tools with 10% bleach solution between each plant.
Avoid working in fields when foliage is wet to prevent bacterial spread.
Use staking and trellising to keep plants off the ground.
biological: Apply Pseudomonas fluorescens (10g/L) as seed treatment and foliar spray.
Use Bacillus subtilis bio-bactericide for competitive exclusion of pathogens.
Introduce plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria (PGPR) in soil.
Apply vermicompost tea as foliar bio-stimulant to boost plant immunity.

spray.best_time: Early morning (6:00 – 8:00 AM) when dew has dried
spray.wind_warning: Do not spray during rain — bacteria spread through water splash

prevention: Use certified pathogen-free seeds and transplants from trusted nurseries.
Practice crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops for at least 2 years.
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation — use drip irrigation only.
Do not work in fields when plants are wet from dew or rain.
Sanitize all tools, trays, and greenhouse surfaces with 10% bleach.
Remove and destroy all crop residues after harvest to eliminate bacterial reservoirs.
tips: Bacterial Spot lesions are small, dark, and water-soaked — unlike fungal spots which are dry.
Copper sprays are preventive, not curative — start spraying before symptoms appear.
Hot, humid weather with frequent rain is peak season for Bacterial Spot outbreaks.
Wash hands with soap before and after handling infected plants to prevent spread.
bacterial_spot.source: University of Florida IFAS Extension; APS Compendium of Tomato Diseases

organic: Spray milk solution (40% milk in water) every 5-7 days as foliar treatment.
Apply potassium bicarbonate (3g/L) with wetting agent for surface pH control.
Use sulfur-based organic fungicide (Wettable Sulfur 80% WP at 3g/L).
Apply neem oil (5ml/L) combined with baking soda for dual-mode action.
chemical: Spray Dinocap 48% EC at 1ml/L as contact fungicide against mildew.
Apply Hexaconazole 5% EC at 2ml/L for systemic curative action.
Use Azoxystrobin 23% SC at 1ml/L for broad-spectrum strobilurin control.
Alternate triazole and strobilurin groups to prevent resistance.
mechanical: Remove heavily infected leaves and dispose of them away from the field.
Improve plant spacing and prune dense canopy for better air circulation.
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization which promotes soft, susceptible growth.
Water at soil level — avoid wetting foliage during irrigation.
biological: Apply Ampelomyces quisqualis (AQ10) bio-fungicide — a hyperparasite of powdery mildew.
Use Bacillus pumilus strain QST 2808 as preventive bio-fungicide.
Introduce Trichoderma harzianum in soil to enhance systemic plant resistance.
Apply dilute whey spray (10%) as a foliar bio-control measure.

spray.best_time: Early morning (6:00 – 9:00 AM) or late evening
spray.wind_warning: Powdery mildew thrives in dry conditions — spray during dry weather

prevention: Plant powdery mildew-resistant cultivars when available.
Ensure adequate plant spacing (45-60cm) for air movement.
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization — use balanced NPK ratios.
Prune lower leaves and dense growth to reduce humidity around foliage.
Apply preventive sulfur spray at flowering stage in susceptible crops.
Monitor humidity levels — powdery mildew thrives at 60-80% relative humidity.
tips: White powdery coating on upper leaf surfaces is the hallmark — check both sides.
Unlike most fungi, Powdery Mildew does NOT need water on leaves to germinate.
Milk spray (40% concentration) is scientifically proven effective as organic control.
Sulfur-based sprays should not be applied when temperature exceeds 35°C.
powdery_mildew.source: UC Davis IPM; ICAR-Indian Institute of Horticultural Research

organic: Apply copper-based fungicide (Bordeaux mixture 0.5%) every 10 days.
Spray neem oil (5ml/L) to suppress fungal spore germination.
Use baking soda spray (1 tbsp/gallon) to raise leaf surface pH.
Apply Trichoderma-based bio-fungicide as preventive foliar spray.
chemical: Spray Mancozeb 75% WP at 2.5g/L as contact preventive fungicide.
Apply Chlorothalonil 75% WP at 2g/L every 7-10 days.
Use Azoxystrobin 23% SC at 1ml/L for systemic control in greenhouses.
Apply Difenoconazole 25% EC at 0.5ml/L as curative systemic treatment.
mechanical: Improve greenhouse ventilation — open vents and side panels during daytime.
Remove lower infected leaves and maintain clean plant canopy.
Reduce plant density to allow air movement between plants.
Avoid overhead watering — use drip irrigation exclusively.
biological: Apply Bacillus subtilis bio-fungicide as preventive foliar spray.
Use Trichoderma viride (5g/L) for competitive exclusion of Cladosporium.
Introduce Pseudomonas fluorescens as seed and soil treatment.
Apply compost tea rich in beneficial microorganisms.

spray.best_time: Early morning (7:00 – 9:00 AM) after greenhouse ventilation
spray.evening_alternative: Not recommended — high humidity at night worsens leaf mold
spray.wind_warning: Ensure greenhouse ventilation fans are running during spraying

prevention: Maintain greenhouse humidity below 85% using ventilation and dehumidifiers.
Use resistant tomato varieties (e.g., varieties with Cf resistance genes).
Space plants adequately (60cm) to ensure air circulation.
Water at soil level early morning to reduce evening leaf wetness.
Remove all infected debris at end of growing season.
Sterilize greenhouse structures and tools between growing seasons.
tips: Yellow patches on upper leaf surface with olive-green mold underneath confirm Leaf Mold.
Greenhouse tomatoes are most susceptible — open-field crops rarely get Leaf Mold.
Relative humidity above 85% is the primary driver — control humidity first.
Prune lower leaves up to the first fruit truss to improve airflow.
leaf_mold.source: Cornell University Vegetable MD Online; CABI Invasive Species Compendium

organic: Apply sulfur-based fungicide (Wettable Sulfur 3g/L) as preventive spray.
Use neem oil (5ml/L) combined with copper for organic rust control.
Spray potassium bicarbonate (3g/L) to suppress rust pustule development.
Apply compost tea as foliar bio-stimulant to boost natural plant defenses.
chemical: Spray Propiconazole 25% EC at 1ml/L for systemic triazole control.
Apply Mancozeb 75% WP at 2.5g/L as contact protective fungicide.
Use Azoxystrobin 23% SC at 1ml/L if rust is spreading rapidly.
Apply Tebuconazole 25.9% EC at 1ml/L for curative treatment.
mechanical: Remove and destroy heavily infected lower leaves to reduce spore load.
Maintain clean field borders — remove grassy weed hosts near crop.
Practice crop residue management — plow under infected stubble after harvest.
Ensure proper plant spacing for air circulation between rows.
biological: Apply Trichoderma harzianum (5g/L) as preventive soil and foliar treatment.
Use Bacillus subtilis bio-fungicide for systemic resistance induction.
Introduce beneficial soil fungi through organic compost amendments.
Apply silicon-rich foliar spray (potassium silicate 2g/L) to harden leaf surface.

spray.best_time: Early morning (6:00 – 9:00 AM) when dew has dried
spray.wind_warning: Rust spores are wind-borne — spray during calm conditions

prevention: Plant rust-resistant hybrid varieties recommended for your region.
Avoid late planting — early planted crops escape peak rust spore season.
Remove grassy weed hosts (alternate hosts) from field borders.
Practice crop rotation with non-cereal crops (legumes, oilseeds).
Scout fields regularly during tasseling and silking stages.
Apply preventive fungicide at first sign of pustules on lower leaves.
tips: Small reddish-brown pustules (like cinnamon powder) on both leaf surfaces confirm rust.
Rust development accelerates between 15-25°C with heavy dew — monitor weather.
If more than 50% of ear-leaf is covered with pustules, economic yield loss is likely.
Fungicide application at VT (tasseling) stage gives best return on investment.
common_rust.source: Purdue University Extension; CIMMYT Maize Disease Handbook

organic: Apply Trichoderma-based bio-fungicide (10g/L) as seed treatment and foliar spray.
Use silicon-rich amendments (rice husk ash) to strengthen plant cell walls.
Spray Pseudomonas fluorescens (10g/L) as preventive bio-control agent.
Apply neem cake (250 kg/ha) as soil amendment with anti-fungal properties.
chemical: Spray Tricyclazole 75% WP at 0.6g/L for preventive systemic protection.
Apply Isoprothiolane 40% EC at 1.5ml/L for curative systemic action.
Use Carbendazim 50% WP at 1g/L as emergency curative treatment.
Apply Kasugamycin 3% SL at 2ml/L for blast and bacterial dual control.
mechanical: Drain paddy fields periodically to reduce humidity at canopy level.
Remove infected tillers and panicles to reduce inoculum source.
Maintain recommended seedling spacing (20x15cm) to reduce humidity.
Practice balanced fertilization — avoid excess nitrogen (>120 kg N/ha).
biological: Apply Pseudomonas fluorescens (10g/L) as seed treatment before sowing.
Use Trichoderma viride (5g/L) as nursery bed treatment.
Introduce Bacillus subtilis for induced systemic resistance.

spray.best_time: Early morning (6:00 – 8:00 AM) before temperature rises
spray.wind_warning: Blast spores travel long distances by wind — regional monitoring important

prevention: Use blast-resistant rice varieties recommended by ICAR/local research stations.
Treat seeds with Tricyclazole or bio-agent before sowing.
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization — split N application in 3 doses.
Maintain proper water management — avoid continuous flooding.
Remove weed hosts and crop residues that harbor blast fungus.
Monitor weather — blast is severe during cloudy, cool nights with heavy dew.
Apply silicon fertilizer (diatomaceous earth) to harden leaf epidermis.
tips: Diamond-shaped lesions with gray center and brown border on leaves confirm blast.
Neck blast (infection at panicle base) causes complete grain loss in that panicle.
Cool nights (20-25°C) with high humidity (>90%) are peak blast conditions.
Spraying at booting/heading stage is critical to prevent neck blast.
Report severe blast outbreaks to district agricultural officer for regional advisory.
rice_blast.source: IRRI International Rice Research Institute; ICAR-National Rice Research Institute

organic: Spray lime sulfur (1:40 dilution) during dormant season as preventive.
Apply copper-based fungicide at green tip stage (before bloom).
Use sulfur-based fungicide (3g/L) every 7 days during wet spring weather.
Apply neem oil (5ml/L) as supplemental foliar treatment.
chemical: Spray Mancozeb 75% WP at 2.5g/L as protective contact fungicide.
Apply Myclobutanil 10% WP at 0.4g/L as systemic curative treatment.
Use Captan 50% WP at 2g/L as broad-spectrum protective spray.
Apply Difenoconazole 25% EC at 0.5ml/L post-infection as kickback treatment.
mechanical: Rake and destroy fallen scab-infected leaves in autumn to reduce overwintering inoculum.
Prune trees to open canopy for better air circulation and faster leaf drying.
Apply urea (5%) to fallen leaves in autumn to accelerate decomposition.
Remove severely scabbed fruits to prevent secondary infections.
biological: Apply Bacillus subtilis bio-fungicide as preventive foliar spray.
Use Trichoderma-enriched compost mulch around tree base.
Introduce Cladosporium cladosporioides as competitive mycoparasite.
Apply compost tea as foliar bio-stimulant to enhance phyllosphere diversity.

spray.best_time: Before and during rain events — scab needs rain for infection
spray.evening_alternative: Spray before predicted rain in the forecast
spray.wind_warning: Scab ascospores release during rain — spray before rain, not after

prevention: Plant scab-resistant apple varieties (Liberty, Enterprise, GoldRush).
Remove and destroy fallen leaves in autumn — primary inoculum source.
Prune trees annually for open canopy and rapid leaf drying.
Apply dormant-season lime sulfur spray before bud break.
Monitor weather — infection occurs during wet periods lasting 9+ hours.
Maintain orchard floor clean with mowing and leaf shredding.
tips: Olive-green velvety spots on leaves and corky scabs on fruit confirm Apple Scab.
Primary infection window is from green tip to petal fall — most critical spray period.
Rain + 9 hours of continuous leaf wetness = infection event (Mills Table).
Post-harvest infected fruit in storage develops storage scab — sort carefully.
apple_scab.source: Cornell University Plant Pathology; Washington State University Tree Fruit

organic: No treatment required — continue regular organic maintenance practices.
Apply compost or vermicompost as soil health maintenance amendment.
chemical: No chemical treatment needed for healthy plants.
Consider preventive foliar micronutrient spray (Zinc + Boron) for optimal growth.
mechanical: Continue regular pruning and canopy management for optimal growth.
Maintain clean field surroundings and remove weed competitors.
biological: Apply Trichoderma or Pseudomonas bio-agents as preventive soil health treatment.
Maintain soil organic matter through green manure and cover cropping.

spray.evening_alternative: Apply preventive bio-agent spray during cooler hours if desired

prevention: Continue balanced NPK fertilization as per crop growth stage.
Maintain proper irrigation scheduling based on soil moisture readings.
Practice crop rotation to maintain soil health and break pest cycles.
Scout fields weekly for early detection of any emerging pest or disease.
Keep field borders clean and free from weed hosts.
Apply preventive bio-agents (Trichoderma, Pseudomonas) every 3 weeks.
tips: Your crop is healthy! Maintain current management practices.
Regular field scouting helps catch problems early before they spread.
Balanced nutrition is key — avoid over-fertilization, especially excess nitrogen.
Keep detailed crop records for better planning in future seasons.
